text: # Teaching Robots to Drive: Scalable Policy Improvement via Human Feedback > Abstract A long-standing problem in autonomous driving is grappling with the long-tail of rare scenarios for which little or no data is available. Although learning-based methods scale with data, it is unclear that simply ramping up data collection will eventually make this problem go away. Approaches which rely on simulation or world modeling offer some relief, but building such models is very challenging and in itself an active area of research. On the other hand, humans can learn to drive without millions of logged driving miles or the ability to precisely predict the trajectories of all dynamic actors in the scene. This suggests a potential alternative path to learning robust driving policies which does not rely on highly accurate world models or enormous driving datasets – one which leans into human preferences and expertise as an untapped source of supervision for training driving policies. This thesis aims to make the case for human feedback as a rich signal for improving driving policies in a sample efficient manner without requiring high fidelity simulation. First, we propose a method for guiding driving policies at test-time using unseen black-box reward functions. We can then synthesize reward functions using natural language and optimize them online, allowing us to solve novel tasks zero-shot using only language supervision. Next, we show how driving policies can be fine-tuned offline using human preference data. By eliciting preferences over high-level intents, we can use human feedback to effectively relabel sub-optimal driving demonstrations and improve on-road driving performance. As future work, we aim to combine these two methods to finetune driving policies offline using natural language corrections, which should enable richer feedback over longer horizons and chain-of-thought distillation.

# Introduction

A long-standing problem in autonomous driving is grappling with the long-tail of rare scenarios. While modern AV approaches have seen major advances in recent years for everyday driving, the real challenge lies in tackling edge cases for which samples are risky to collect or non-existent. Especially in safety-critical situations, gracefully handling these scenarios is crucial for reliable autonomy. While these issue is pervasive across the AV stack, in this work we will primarily focus on planning and policy learning, i.e., how should we learn to act when confronted with the long-tail of driving scenarios?

Conventional autonomy systems rely on rule-based planning and heuristics in lieu of end-to-end learning [[15]](#page-39-0). One major advantage of these approaches is that since they do not rely on learning from data, and do not have the same issues with generalization that learning-based methods do. However, these systems are still susceptible to the long-tail as these heuristics are not perfect, and carefully tuning these methods to improve performance on edge cases without hurting performance in other areas is a laborious task.

In recent years, we have seen the rise of learning-based planning approaches which alleviate the need for manually adapting heuristics and rules by learning directly from expert driving logs [2, 3, 9, 10, 12, 13, 37, [89]](#page-46-0). Although learning-based methods scale with data, it is unclear that simply scaling up data collection will solve the long-tail. Given the complexity of real open-world urban driving scenes, there is enormous potential for encountering novel situations and a vanishingly small chance that the

same situation will occur twice. As driving agents improve, safety-critical encounters will also become increasingly rare. Even for scenarios for which a limited number of samples are available, merely fine-tuning on these samples with imitation learning may rely on heuristically inferring corrective actions and/or data re-balancing.

However, building high-fidelity world models for driving is challenging and remains an active area of research. In general, human driving behaviors are highly stochastic and involve coordination with other drivers in nontrivial ways. Additionally, reactive simulation is even harder since we are unable to collect data on counterfactual trajectories, i.e., what would have happened if a specific vehicle had behaved differently. Even evaluating learned world models is difficult for this reason [[44]](#page-41-1). Training policies using learned models also requires special attention since policies may learn to exploit learned models in an adversarial manner [[31]](#page-40-1). In many ways, learning an optimal driving policy directly is an easier proposition than learning a high-fidelity world model for driving.

On the other hand, humans can learn to drive without millions of logged driving miles or the ability to precisely predict the trajectories of all dynamic actors in the scene. This can be partially attributed to our ability to leverage feedback from experts without relying on firsthand experience. Additionally, humans generally rely on heuristics and intuition while driving, and explicit planning can be done efficiently because it utilizes the right abstractions. This suggests a potential alternative path to learning robust driving policies which does not rely on highly accurate world models or enormous driving datasets – one which leans into human preferences and intuitions as a rich source of supervision for training driving policies.

Human feedback can provide a much richer training signal for agents on a persample basis when compared to imitation learning and reinforcement learning. Given a rare scenario, behavior cloning would require many expert demonstrations for the policy to adapt. Reinforcement learning can theoretically obviate the need for expert demonstrations, but generally has even worse sample complexity than imitation learning. However, natural language corrections (e.g. "change lanes here because the car in front is slowing") can supervise not only what should be done at a high-level, but also why this is the case. Supervising the intermediate thought process and

abstractions used during planning is just one way that learning from human feedback can enable much more general driving agents.

text: # Diffusion-ES: Gradient-free Planning with Diffusion for Autonomous Driving and Zero-Shot Instruction Following > 2.1 Introduction Diffusion models have shown to excel at modeling highly complex and multimodal trajectory distributions for decision-making and control [1, [32]](#page-40-2). Reward-gradient guidance [32, 39, [74]](#page-44-0) has been used to test-time optimize differentiable reward functions by alternating between denoising diffusion steps and backpropagating reward gradients to the noised trajectory. In this way, sampled trajectories are pushed towards the trajectory data manifold while also maximizing the reward function at hand [[32]](#page-40-2). This decoupling of the reward function from trajectory diffusion permits a single trajectory diffusion model to be used for maximizing a variety of reward functions at test time. Reward-gradient guidance requires the reward function to be differentiable and fitted in both noisy and clean trajectories, which usually requires re-training. This limits its applicability as a general solver for trajectory optimization. We propose Diffusion-ES, a reward-guided denoising method for optimization of non-differentiable, black-box objectives that samples and mutates trajectories using a diffusion model, guided by a reward function that operates only on the clean, final, denoised samples. Naively combining diffusion with sampling-based optimization does not work: sampling-based optimizers, like CEM [[60]](#page-43-0) or MPPI [[80]](#page-45-0), typically require a large population of samples across multiple iterations of selection and mutation to converge to good solutions, which, when combined with the computational cost of denoising inference, results in a prohibitively slow search process. In Diffusion-ES, high-scoring trajectories are mutated using a truncated diffusion-denoising process, by adding a small amount of noise and denoising them back, as shown in Figure 2.1 right. The amount of added noise is progressively decreased across search iterations making Diffusion-ES computationally viable.

text: # Diffusion-ES: Gradient-free Planning with Diffusion for Autonomous Driving and Zero-Shot Instruction Following > 2.1 Introduction > 2.2 Related work Diffusion models for decision-making and trajectory optimization Diffusion models [26, 48, 68, [69]](#page-44-3) learn to approximate the data distribution through an iterative denoising process and have shown impressive results on image generation [16, 55, 59, [61]](#page-43-5). They have been used for imitation learning for manipulation tasks [11, 50, 57, [81]](#page-45-1), for controllable vehicle motion generation [7, 34, [91]](#page-46-1) and for video generation of manipulation tasks [19, [85]](#page-45-2). Works of [35, [92]](#page-46-2) use diffusion models to forecast offline vehicle trajectories. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to use diffusion models in closed-loop driving. Learning versus planning for autonomous driving Learning to drive from imitating driving demonstrations is prevalent in the research and development of autonomous vehicles [2, 3, 9, 10, 13, 37, 52, 53, 56, [90]](#page-46-3). Many preeminent imitation methods assume the underlying action distribution is unimodal, which is problematic when training from multimodal expert demonstrations. Objectives and architectures that can better handle multimodal trajectory prediction have been proposed [14, 21, 46, 65, 71? ]. We show that diffusion models are well-suited for driving and can be used to synthesize rich complex behaviors from multimodal demonstrations.

Specifically, we use a trained diffusion model ϵθ to initialize the sample population and we use a truncated diffuse-denoise process to mutate samples while staying in the data manifold. The control flow of Diffusion-ES is shown in Figure 2.1 (left). Initializing the population with diffusion sampling We begin by sampling an initial population X0 of M trajectory samples using our diffusion model: X 0 = {xi} M i=1 ∼ pθ(x), (2.1) where Xk is the population at iteration k. Given we use an unconditional diffusion model, these samples are scene agnostic and can always be used without re-sampling them at each timestep. Sample scoring At each iteration k, we score the samples in our population {R(xi)|xi ∈ Xk} M i=1. Note that our population consists of "clean" samples so we do not need a reward function which can handle "noisy" samples, which gives us significant flexibility compared to guidance methods that perform classifier-based guidance. text: # Diffusion-ES: Gradient-free Planning with Diffusion for Autonomous Driving and Zero-Shot Instruction Following > 2.1 Introduction > 2.4 Experiments We first evaluate Diffusion-ES on closed-loop driving in nuPlan [[6]](#page-38-3), an established benchmark that uses estimated perception for vehicles, pedestrians, lanes and traffic signs. Our model and baselines are evaluated on their ability to drive safely and efficiently while having access to close-to-ground-truth perception output provided by the dataset. We also consider a suite of driving instruction following tasks. We map instructions to shaped reward functions with LLM prompting, and evaluate Diffusion-ES and baselines in their ability to optimize the generated reward functions and accurately follow the instructions. Our experiments aim to answer the following questions: - 1. How does Diffusion-ES compare to existing sampling-based planners and reward-gradient guidance for trajectory optimization? - 2. How does Diffusion-ES compare to SOTA reactive driving policies that directly map environments' state to vehicle trajectories? - 3. Can the hardest nuPlan driving scenarios be solved by assuming access to a human teacher giving instructions in natural language, without any additional training data? - 4. Does scene conditioning for the diffusion model benefit Diffusion-ES?

text: # Diffusion-ES: Gradient-free Planning with Diffusion for Autonomous Driving and Zero-Shot Instruction Following > 2.1 Introduction > 2.4 Experiments > 2.4.1 Closed-loop driving We evaluate our model on the nuPlan Val14 planning benchmark [[15]](#page-39-0). We specifically consider the reactive agent track of the nuPlan benchmark since it is the most difficult and realistic of the evaluation settings in nuPlan. Model setup and hyperparameters For Diffusion-ES, we train a diffusion model over ego-vehicle trajectories consisting of 2D poses (x, y, θ) predicted 8 seconds into the future at 2Hz, leading to an overall action dimension of 48. Unlike prior work [[32]](#page-40-2), we model the distribution over actions only rather than modeling states and actions. We use a population size of M = 128 in our experiments. Our diffusion model is trained with T = 100 denoising steps. Reward function We adopt a modified version of the scoring function used in PDM-Closed [[15]](#page-39-0) as our reward function. To compute rewards, we convert our predicted trajectory to low-level control inputs using an LQR tracker. These control inputs are fed into a kinematic bicycle model [[51]](#page-42-7) which propagates the dynamics of the ego-vehicle. We follow [[15]](#page-39-0) and forecast the motion of other agents by assuming constant velocity. These simulated rollouts are then scored following the nuPlan benchmark evaluation metrics. We also add auxiliary reward terms to penalize proximity to the leading agent and enforce speed limits. Note that this reward function is not differentiable due to the tracker and the use of non-differentiable heuristics for assessing traffic violations. text: # Diffusion-ES: Gradient-free Planning with Diffusion for Autonomous Driving and Zero-Shot Instruction Following > 2.1 Introduction > 2.4 Experiments > 2.4.2 Language instruction following One drawback of the nuPlan driving benchmark is that encourages highly conservative driving behaviors. For example, PDM-Closed [[15]](#page-39-0) holds the state-of-the-art in the nuPlan Val14 benchmark while being unable to change lanes, since its path proposals only consider the lane the ego-vehicle is currently on. However, lane changing is not necessary for good driving performance in the current nuPlan benchmark. To evaluate Diffusion-ES and baselines in their ability to optimize arbitrary reward functions, we consider eight language instruction following tasks, each taken from an existing driving log in the nuPlan benchmark. In each task, the language instruction requires the ego-vehicle to perform a specific driving maneuver that solves a challenging driving scenario. In most scenarios there will be no examples of the instructed behavior anywhere in nuPlan. For instance, the lane weaving task requires the ego-vehicle to aggressively change multiple lanes in dense urban traffic. Task descriptions, language instructions, and prompts are provided in the appendix. We use the method described in 2.3.3 to generate executable Python code given a language instruction that adapts the initial reward function of Section 2.4.1, giving us a language-shaped reward function for each scenario. Our model and baselines will optimize the same language-shaped reward function. Evaluation metric We evaluate our model and baselines using task success rate, which measures how frequently the agent was able to successfully complete the designated task. To increase the difficulty of the tasks, we randomize the behavior of other vehicle agents by adding noise to their IDM parameters at sporadic intervals during each episode. All scores reported are averaged across ten random seeds. Baselines We compare to the following baselines: - PDM-Closed: this is adapted to this setting by using our language-shaped reward function in place of the original reward function. - PDM-Closed-Multilane: a modified variant of PDM-Closed which considers a wider range of laterally offset paths, allowing for lane changes. - Conditional Diffusion-ES: Diffusion-ES that uses a conditional diffusion model instead of an unconditional one.

We believe that these issues can be mitigated by incorporating recent advances in diffusion modeling such as faster samplers. Our reward function assumes other agents will travel at constant velocity, which could clearly be improved. This also assumes that other agents cannot react to the ego-vehicle, which has been shown to be a major limitation for planners in self-driving [[58]](#page-43-7). However, our instruction following experiments suggest that even if we cannot ever forecast perfectly, we can use language-shaped rewards to solve the hardest driving scenarios.

text: # Diffusion-ES: Gradient-free Planning with Diffusion for Autonomous Driving and Zero-Shot Instruction Following > 2.1 Introduction > 2.5 Conclusion We presented Diffusion-ES, a method for black-box reward guided diffusion sampling. We showed that Diffusion-ES can effectively optimize reward functions in nuPlan for driving and instruction following, and outperforms engineered sampling-based planners, reactive deterministic or diffusion policies, as well as differentiable rewardgradient guidance. We showed how our method can be used to follow language instructions without any language-action trajectory data, simply using LLM prompting to generate shaped reward maps for test-time optimization. Our future work will explore retrieving the right reward shaping to optimize to handle long-tailed driving scenarios in the absence of human teachers. Our experiments show the trade-off between inference speed and OOD generalization during scene conditioning in diffusion policies.

heading_path: Latent Preference Finetuning for Driving Policies
text: # Latent Preference Finetuning for Driving Policies > 3.1 Introduction In the previous work, we showed how online natural language instructions can be used to guide driving agents. However, we are interested in how human feedback can be used to improve policies over time. In this work, we propose initial work towards improving driving policies from offline human preference feedback. Rather than learn directly from open-ended natural language feedback, we focus on learning from preferences over discrete high-level intentions (e.g., "change lanes to the left", "slow down", "accelerate") for a few reasons. First, it is significantly faster and easier for human labelers to select the most desirable high-level intent versus asking for a natural language correction. In special cases, it may even be possible to extract such labels programmatically without relying on manual human labeling. Next, since the intent-space is discrete and enumerable, learning models over these preferences is much easier than modeling preferences over unstructured text. We can also assume that the human can identify the global "best" intent, as opposed to in conventional RLHF settings where preference labels are only locally relevant and require more complex methods for extracting usable reward models. We propose a novel technique for fine-tuning driving policies using human latent preferences (i.e., preferences over high-level intents). Given a two-stage policy which consists of a high-level latent policy and a low-level policy conditioned on a high-level latent, we use preference labels to supervise the high-level policy using intent-specific high-level policies. This allows us to refine driving policies using only high-level feedback. We find that these procedure leads to improved driving performance when tested on real-world driving tasks. Since this work is going, we will omit discussion of current experimental results.

text: # Latent Preference Finetuning for Driving Policies > 3.2 Related Work There has been substantial work in aligning language models with human preferences [49, [54]](#page-42-9). In the conventional RLHF setting, preference data is generated by sampling completions from a pretrained model and asking a human labeler to rank them. This is usually done after pretraining on large amounts of internet-scale data and supervised fine-tuning on task-specific data. Since preference labels provide less training signal than imitating "ground-truth" samples, these methods rely on theoretical preference models such as Bradley-Terry [[4]](#page-38-8) to extract reward models [[49]](#page-42-8) or policy gradients [[54]](#page-42-9). As mentioned earlier, we choose to focus on categorical intent preferences in this work due to ease of optimization and data collection. Separately, there is recent work in building interactive robotic agents which can improve from human feedback [40, 67, [75]](#page-44-8). Most closely related to our approach is YAY Robot [[67]](#page-44-7), which uses human language supervision to guide a low-level language-conditioned policy for manipulation. While the motivation is similar, we opt for categorical intent latents due to the difficulty of collecting large amounts of high-quality language corrections in our setting. Training language-conditioned driving policies is highly non-trivial and we leave this to future work. Another related work is SkiP [[75]](#page-44-8), which uses human feedback both for skill extraction and policy improvement. However, SkiP focuses on a preference learning setup which is more reminiscent of prior work in RLHF as the human not asked to uniquely identify the best skill to execute. One major difference which differentiates our work from the above is also that whereas they mostly consider smaller datasets on the order of thousands of samples, we scale up our approach to handle several orders of magnitude more data. ![](images/_page_30_Diagram_1.jpeg) Figure 3.1: Architecture diagram for end-to-end two-stage driving policy.

text: # Latent Preference Finetuning for Driving Policies > 3.3 Method > 3.3.1 Model Architecture The architecture for our driving policy is outlined in Figure 3.1. Our observation o consists of driving inputs (e.g., camera images, route map), with two past frames included for temporal context. Additionally, we include frames from three front-facing cameras to cover a wider field of view. Our policy processes the observation with a learned state encoder backbone and uses these state features for both the high-level latent policy and the low-level policy. This two-stage policy uses discretized 2-second waypoint goals zwp as intermediate latent actions (i.e., the (x, y) position of the ego-vehicle after 2 seconds). We assume an 11 × 11 binning of waypoint goals in log-polar coordinates. Our low-level actions a are 2D waypoint trajectories sampled at 5 Hz with a horizon of 2 seconds, so we can extract our high-level latent zwp by taking the last waypoint in the low-level action and applying binning. The high-level policy πwp(zwp|o) is trained to predict the ground-truth waypoint goal bin, which amounts to cross-entropy minimization. The low-level policy πout(a|o, zwp) takes the ground-truth latent action as input is trained to predict a Gaussian which maximizes the likelihood of the ground-truth trajectory action. We train the above model using behavior cloning and measure the performance of our proposed finetuning method with respect to this base policy. During preference finetuning, we freeze the state encoder and low-level policy and only finetune the high-level policy.

text: # Latent Preference Finetuning for Driving Policies > 3.3 Method > 3.3.2 Intent Policy Finetuning In this section we discuss how we train intent-specific latent policies, as well as how those policies are used for latent preference finetuning. We introduce an intent latent: zint ∼ Categorical(K) where there are K total possible mutually exclusive intents, each representing a high-level behavior such (e.g., "overtaking", "slowing", "accelerating"). While we could theoretically perform preference finetuning using the spatial waypoint latents introduced previously, we found that it was challenging for human annotators to provide high-quality labels for spatial waypoints. On the other hand, high-level intents are easier to interpret and label due to their semantic nature. Using the above, we construct an intent-conditioned high-level policy. In practice, this can be implemented by training a mixture of K high-level policies, one for each intent: π(zwp|o, zint) = X i 1(zint = i)π(zwp|o, zint = i) We find that using a single shared policy can lead to the intent-conditioning not being used, whereas training separate policies avoids collapse. This suggests a natural scheme for finetuning using preference labels over intents. For a given intent label zint = i, we can use our intent-conditioned high-level policy to generate a new target zˆwp ∼ π(zwp|o, zint = i) for supervising the high-level policy in our original model. Note that this allows us to generate labels for trajectories where the demonstrations are not expert as well.

heading_path: 4.1 Finetuning Driving Policies with Natural Language
text: # Future Work > 4.1 Finetuning Driving Policies with Natural Language > 4.1.1 Motivation While categorical intent preferences are conceptually simpler, there are substantial advantages to eliciting human feedback in the form of natural language. Natural language has the potential to be a much richer training signal than preferences over discrete intentions. Many of the intents used in chapter 3 correspond to behaviors which are meaningful over the planning horizon (2 seconds), but this restricts us to fairly myopic policy feedback. For instance, situations such as four-way stops require slightly longer temporal contexts, and handling such scenarios is very clunky when using the current approach. Language corrections are more open-ended and allow for planning over multiple timescales. Additionally, simply selecting the right intent does not necessarily dictate why that choice is correct, and this kind of supervision is not easy to do with the current latent preference finetuning approach. There has been some work towards training language-conditioned policies [[66]](#page-44-9), and such policies could be used to synthesize corrective actions from offline language feedback. However, training such policies is challenging as they generally do not perform better than equivalent policies without language conditioning. The question remains: how can we leverage language feedback without compromising on performance?

heading_path: 4.1 Finetuning Driving Policies with Natural Language
text: # Future Work > 4.1 Finetuning Driving Policies with Natural Language > 4.1.2 Method Drawing from Diffusion-ES [[84]](#page-45-8) and Code-as-Policies [[38]](#page-41-7), we can use few-shot LLM prompting to map language instructions to corrective actions. As was demonstrated in chapter 2, leveraging the coding abilities of LLMs allows us to handle a much richer set of language commands which can be flexibly composed in ways unseen at training time. Specifically, we can replace the reward shaping API from Diffusion-ES with an action API which uses the intent-specific policies as callable functions. Therefore, while each language instruction is mapped to a specific intent at each timestep, language instructions can control the conditions under which each intent ought to be used. Since much of the difficulty in driving is not in low-level control (e.g., "how to move into the right lane") but in high-level decisionmaking (e.g., "when is it safe to change lanes"), this should not be a significant restriction on the expressiveness of these code policies. In Diffusion-ES, the perception API was hard-coded because we assumed groundtruth perception (i.e., perfect bounding-boxes, HD maps, etc.). However, in the experimental setting from chapter 3 we do not have access to these perception outputs. One proposed fix could be to use pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to handle perception. This also allows us to garner the benefits of large-scale foundation models which can handle open-world perception queries without task-specific finetuning. There have been several works which propose to use LLMs / VLMs in a similar fashion [72, [73]](#page-44-11).

text: # Future Work > 4.2 Preference Finetuning via Chain-of-Thought Distillation > 4.2.1 Motivation As mentioned in the previous section, one of the advantages of using language feedback is process supervision – human annotators can supervise not only the output action, but the process for reaching that action. This line of work is directly inspired by procedure cloning [[86]](#page-45-9), which showed that training agents to imitate intermediate computations (e.g. BFS visitations) leads to much stronger test set performance compared to imitating only the final output. Chain-of-thought prompting is a closely related technique which has become ubiquitous for LLM prompting [[78]](#page-45-10). This suggests that effectively incorporating this intermediate supervision via language feedback may considerably boost generalization. Our current latent preference finetuning procedure only uses the final outputs of the intent-conditioned latent policy for supervision, and this holds true for related approaches which learn from human feedback [67, [75]](#page-44-8). One work which uses chain-of-thought supervision is CoTPC [[33]](#page-41-11), which treats detected change-points as intermediate computations for auxiliary decoding, but does not incorporate language supervision.

heading_path: 4.2 Preference Finetuning via Chain-of-Thought Distillation
text: # Future Work > 4.2 Preference Finetuning via Chain-of-Thought Distillation > 4.2.2 Method Unlike maze solving or graph traversal, there is no fixed decisionmaking algorithm which humans follow when driving. Additionally, given the open-ended nature of this process, there are potentially many different ways of arriving at the same intent which gives us a lot of flexibility in how this approach could be designed. One possibility is to simply decompose the current high-level latent policy into a language policy and a language-conditioned latent policy similar to YAY Robot [[67]](#page-44-7): π(zwp|o) = π(zlang|o)π(zwp|o, zlang) where zlang is a language embedding. At training time, the language instruction is encoded to obtain a language embedding zwp. This is used to supervise the language policy π(zlang|o) and is provided as input to the language-conditioned latent policy π(zwp|o, zlang). Note that none of this affects the training of the intent-specific policies themselves, only the base policy. This approach is conceptually straightforward but potentially suffers from some of the same issues as training language-conditioned policies in the first place. Training a language policy π(zlang|o) could be quite challenging since there are potentially many valid language instructions for each observation o. This would potentially require a much higher capacity model to adequately handle natural language. Additionally, we already encounter issues now in latent preference finetuning where conditioning on intents and observations leads to the intent variable being ignored – this may be exacerbated when conditioning on language embeddings since they are harder to parse compared to categorical intents.
